newsitem.title: TOGO: LOME SUMMIT COULD MAKE PROGRESS TOWARD ZAIRE PEACE.
newsitem.headline: LOME SUMMIT COULD MAKE PROGRESS TOWARD ZAIRE PEACE.

text.p: Zaire's shaky regime was edging towards its first talks with advancing rebels on Wednesday as African leaders gathered in Togo for a one-day summit on the Zaire crisis.
International pressure on the two sides to stop fighting mounted sharply, personified by the presence of U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan in Lome, the Togolese capital.
"I hope that in Lome we will find a basis for moving forward by perhaps having a ceasefire and talks begin simultaneously," Annan said on Tuesday in Angola.
President Mobutu Sese Seko's camp signalled it was ready to deal with Laurent Kabila's rebels, who have made short shrift of Zaire's ragged army in a five-month campaign.
"We shall meet and after dialogue we will share power," Banza Mukalayi, vice-chairman of Mobutu's MPR party, told Reuters in Kinshasa.
"First we will talk to find the mechanism for a ceasefire and then we will share power before elections," Banza said.
Neither Mobutu nor Kabila is officially due in Lome, where the first presidents arrived on Tuesday ahead of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit.

But both dispatched senior delegations and the prospect of a meeting was taken seriously by diplomats. Kabila's men had no mandate to negotiate but even a preliminary session with Mobutu's aides would be a breakthrough.
Top French and American officials were attending the summit with Annan, whose decision to take part was a surprise and implied progress was possible.

South African President Nelson Mandela, criticised in the past for refusing the lead role in the continent's conflicts, has strongly backed the effort to bring peace in Zaire, sending envoys to both sides in the past week.
Vice-President Thabo Mbeki will attend the Lome summit after apparently persuading Kabila to accept the principle of talks with Mobutu's top lieutenants instead of the 66-year-old leader himself.
The potential break-up of Africa's third biggest country, with nine neighbours, is a nightmare diplomats want to avoid.
More than 1,000 American, French and Belgian troops were massed in Congo, one of those neighbours, ready to evacuate Westerners from Zaire if necessary.
Rebel sympathisers were wary of the military build-up, fearing it could turn into a bid to shore up what is left of Mobutu's 32-year-old regime.
In theory Kabila has little reason to stop fighting. His fighters, disciplined and backed by Ugandan and Rwandan troops according to Zaire, already control a quarter of the country.
They are moving steadily against Lubumbashi, capital of the southern province of Shaba whose vast reserves of copper, cobalt and precious metals have made Mobutu's elite super-rich.
Battling prostate cancer and absent in Europe for most of the past eight months, Mobutu seemed far from ready to quit.

In a televised statement on Tuesday night read by his spokesman, the president proposed a complex formula for dealing with the crisis which seemed certain to confuse Kinshasa's squabbling politicians.
Mobutu suggested the creation of a broad-based National Council to "mobilise public opinion" on the need to find peace, and a quite separate committee of actual negotiators.
"It's a classic Mobutu move to get the politicians scrabbling for jobs," a foreign observer in Kinshasa said.

Opposition and pro-Mobutu parties in Kinshasa held a series of meetings to discuss the appointment of a new prime minister after Kengo wa Dondo's resignation on Monday night. Kengo and his team remained in charge in the meantime.
Under Mobutu's laborious and grudging moves towards democracy, Zaire is supposed to hold its first real multiparty elections by July.
The deadline was always far-fetched but five months into the rebellion it looks fanciful. Some Kinshasa politicians argued it was better to talk to Kabila before forming a government.

"Mobutu is trying to save his own skin. We cannot have a government in Kinshasa when we don't know how much territory Kinshasa will control tomorrow," opposition member of parliament Engineer Dyongo said. REUTER
